Bug: s390x ggml_vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1 reads an uninitialised accumulator

### Name and Version

Present on current `master` in `ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/s390/quants.c`. Found while working on a z/OS port of llama.cpp; the file is s390x-only so this affects IBM Z builds.

### Operating systems

Other? (z/OS, and any Linux on IBM Z)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libggml (CPU backend, s390x)

### Problem description

`ggml_vec_dot_q5_1_q8_1()` reads `v_acc` in its own initialiser, before it has been assigned:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/s390/quants.c#L639

```c
const float32x4_t v_d = vec_splats(GGML_CPU_FP16_TO_FP32(x0->d) * GGML_CPU_FP16_TO_FP32(y0->d));
const float32x4_t v_acc = vec_madd(v_xyf, v_d, v_acc);   // <-- v_acc is uninitialised here

sumf += vec_hsum_f32x4(v_acc) + summs;
```

`v_acc` is declared `const` inside the loop body and has no prior value, so the third operand of `vec_madd` is whatever the register happens to hold. The accumulated `sumf` is therefore garbage, and can be NaN or Inf depending on the residue.

The intended form is visible in the structurally identical loop in `ggml_vec_dot_q5_0_q8_0()` a few functions earlier, which seeds the multiply-add with zero:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/s390/quants.c#L486

```c
const float32x4_t v_acc = vec_madd(v_xyf, v_d, vec_splats(0.0f));
```

The two functions differ only in that q5_1 also carries `summs`, so this looks like a copy-paste slip when q5_1 was derived from q5_0.

### Suggested fix

```diff
-        const float32x4_t v_acc = vec_madd(v_xyf, v_d, v_acc);
+        const float32x4_t v_acc = vec_madd(v_xyf, v_d, vec_splats(0.0f));
```

`-Wall` flags it as `variable 'v_acc' is uninitialized when used within its own initialization`.

### Relevant log output

```
Compiler diagnostic:

quants.c:639:35: warning: variable 'v_acc' is uninitialized when used within its own initialization [-Wuninitialized]
        const float32x4_t v_acc = vec_madd(v_xyf, v_d, v_acc);
                          ~~~~~                        ^~~~~
```

Misc. bug: webui does not display image attachments returned by MCP tools (tool block regression in #25450, inline references never resolved)

### Name and Version

version: b10042 (behavior also verified by reading the tools/ui sources at tag b10042)

### Operating systems

All (this is a webui / frontend issue, reproduced on Windows with Chrome)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server with any tool-calling model, webui with an MCP server enabled whose tool returns image content
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I have an MCP server with a tool that returns a static map as a PNG (standard MCP image content: `{ type: "image", mimeType: "image/png", data: "<base64>" }`). The webui extracts the image correctly: the tool result shows a line like `[Attachment saved: mcp-attachment-1752...-1.png]` and the image is stored as an `IMAGE` extra on the tool result message (I can see it in IndexedDB). But the image is never displayed anywhere in the chat. As far as I can tell there are two separate problems:

**1. Regression from #25450: the image no longer shows in the expanded tool call block.**

Before that PR, `ChatMessageAgenticContent.svelte` rendered tool results with `parseToolResultWithImages(section.toolResult, section.toolResultExtras || message?.extra)`, so the extras of the tool message were used and the image was visible when expanding the block. After the refactor into `ChatMessageToolCallBlock` / `ChatMessageToolCallBlockDefault`, the block receives `attachments={message?.extra}`, which are the extras of the anchor assistant message and never contain the MCP images. `section.toolResultExtras` is still populated in `deriveSingleTurnSections` (`tools/ui/src/lib/utils/agentic.ts`) but nothing consumes it anymore, so it is dead code now. This used to work, see for example the report in #20314 where the returned image was displayed to the user in the tool block.

**2. Older problem: inline references to the attachment never resolve.**

When the model references the saved attachment in its answer, for example `![map](mcp-attachment-1752...-1.png)` (which is the natural thing for the model to do given the `[Attachment saved: ...]` marker in the tool output), the reference does not resolve. `rehypeResolveAttachmentImages` also receives `attachments={message?.extra}` (in `ChatMessageAgenticContent.svelte`), so the lookup fails, the img src stays a relative URL, the browser gets a 404 and the user sees the "Image cannot be displayed (open link)" fallback instead of the image. This part predates #25450, I don't think it ever worked.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Enable an MCP server with a tool that returns image content (a static map tool, an image generation tool, anything).
2. Ask the model something that triggers the tool.
3. The tool output contains `[Attachment saved: mcp-attachment-...png]` but expanding the tool call block shows no image.
4. If the model embeds the attachment name in its reply, the "Image cannot be displayed (open link)" placeholder is rendered instead of the image.

Possible fix: in `ChatMessageAgenticContent.svelte` pass a merged attachment pool to the render paths, something like `[...(message?.extra ?? []), ...toolMessages.flatMap((m) => m.extra ?? [])]`. Attachment names are timestamped so collisions should not be an issue. Or at least restore `section.toolResultExtras` for the tool call block. Since the extras are already persisted in IndexedDB, existing conversations would start rendering correctly as soon as the fix lands.

### First Bad Commit

For the tool block regression: 32beb244f (#25450). The inline reference problem is older and as far as I can tell was never working.

### Relevant log output

```shell
Browser console shows a 404 for GET /mcp-attachment-<timestamp>-1.png when the assistant message references the attachment name.
```

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10724, commit 2d8d612e4)

HIP

Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-Q5_K_M (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-GGUF)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When running llama-server in router mode with --models-max 1, the issue occurs under the following conditions: 
1. Send a request to one model (Model A)
2. Wait for the request to finish
3. Send two or more requests, to two or more different models (Models B and C), simultaneously, while the previous model (Model A) is still loaded and idle, or in the process of unloading

Find below a script that will reproduce this issue every time on my machine. I have tested this with different models in different positions, it always results in llama.cpp hanging every time, no matter which models I put in. Attention, change the port to whatever you're using. Disclaimer, most of the code for the test script is AI generated by GLM-5.3, I hope this is still allowed:
```
# 1. Get a model loaded and idle (any short request on the 12B)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9553/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K", "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' > /dev/null

# 2. Waiter A: arrives while 12B is loaded and idle -> marks slot_pending, starts unloading 12B
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9553/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M", "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' > /dev/null &

# 3. Waiter B: simultaneously, while the 12B unload is still in flight (~300ms window)
curl -s --max-time 60 http://127.0.0.1:9553/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0", "input": "will hang forever"}' > /dev/null

# Expected (buggy): router shows Waiter A loaded+idle, GPU idle.
``` 

Interestingly, the llama-server can be motivated to get out of the freeze by sending a request to a different model. Running this command will make the scheduler resume. But this will only work if the model name in this command is anything except the model of Waiter A.
`curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9553/v1/embeddings -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model": "Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0", "input": "nudge"}'`

In the logs, attached below, you can see what happens if I run the reproduction bash script. 
- It first generates [39415] (the gemma-4-12B), which runs fine.
- Then [39403] (the gemma-4-E2B) is created. 39403 finishes fine, but does not get unloaded.
- At 0.47.885.942, I then used the curl command above to evict the gemma-4-E2B, which will result in Qwen3 loading in for both new jobs.

I'm running llama.cpp in router mode using the following command:
```./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server --models-preset "/home/marco/ai/llm/models.ini" --port 9553 --models-max 1```

# Regression: `--lazy-mode auto` halves prompt-processing (pp512) for qwen4exp on Vulkan (AMD iGPU)

## Summary

After commit `257813839` ("llama: improve TENSOR_READ_LAZY handling (#27837)"), the default
`--lazy-mode auto` roughly **halves the prefill throughput** of the qwen4exp architecture
(`Qwen3.8-Flash-Next`, IQ4_XS) on the **Vulkan** backend of an AMD Strix Halo iGPU
(Radeon 8060S / gfx1151). Setting `--lazy-mode off` restores the previous performance.

- Reported build: `0.3.0-dev (build 10723, commit 010be9683)`
- bisected first-bad commit: `257813839`
- Good baseline (before the commit, build 10662 / `18443257a`): pp512 ≈ **429 t/s**

## How to reproduce

Test with `llama-bench`, model `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` IQ4_XS (qwen4exp arch, ~87 GiB),
Vulkan backend, full offload:

```bash
llama-bench -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf -ngl 99 -p 512 -n 128          # lazy-mode auto (default)
llama-bench -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf -ngl 99 -p 512 -n 128 --lazy-mode off
```

### Results (pp512 t/s)

| Configuration | pp512 (t/s) | tg128 (t/s) |
|---|---|---|
| `--lazy-mode auto` (default, HEAD) | **216** | 24.1 |
| `--lazy-mode off` (HEAD) | **406** | 24.2 |
| pre-commit `257813839` (build 10662) | 429 | 25.6 |

Same model, same build, same backend — only the `--lazy-mode` value differs. `tg128`
is unaffected; only prompt processing regresses.

## Environment

- CPU/GPU: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 "Strix Halo" (gfx1151), Radeon 8060S iGPU
- Memory: 128 GB LPDDR5X unified
- Backend: Vulkan (`radv`, mesa 26.0); device detected as
  `Radeon 8060S Graphics (RADV STRIX_HALO)`, uma: 1
- Kernel: `7.2.0-070200-generic`
- Build: Release, `build-vulkan` (CPU native + Vulkan), commit `010be9683`

## Bisect log (first-bad)

```
good: 0b5be7e4a hip: tune rdna 3 mmq config (#26284)     -> pp512 ≈ 410
bad : 257813839 llama: improve TENSOR_READ_LAZY handling (#27837) -> pp512 ≈ 218
```

Note: I also tested reverting the GDN/LID commit `8663224810` ("context: disable
non-fused GDN and LID ops") as a suspected cause — reverting it had no effect, so the
lazy-read commit is the confirmed culprit.

## Suspected cause

`llama_model_loader::lazy_read` now lazily maps tensors during load even for the
`auto` mode. On Vulkan with this iGPU/UMA setup, the lazy-read path likely produces
suboptimal buffer placement (or host-visible staging) for the large embedding/SSM
tensors of the qwen4exp architecture, making the prefill read weights from a slower path.

## Expected behavior

`--lazy-mode auto` should not degrade prompt processing relative to pre-`257813839`
behavior. At minimum, the `auto` heuristic should avoid lazy-reading tensors when the
backend is Vulkan (or when doing so forces a non-device-local buffer on UMA iGPUs).

## Workaround

Add `--lazy-mode off` to the llama-server/llama-bench invocation. This restores pp512
to ~406 t/s (vs 216 with `auto`). Applied in our `start_llamacpp.sh` for all models.

query: Feature Request: vulkan: command-buffer debug labels for GPU profilers ### Prerequisites - [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well. - [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md). - [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed). - [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share. ### Feature Description While profiling models with the Vulkan backend using the Radeon GPU Profiler (RGP), I noticed the compute dispatches appear without descriptive labels; they are all listed as generic `vkCmdDispatch(N,M,K)` entries. The `VK_EXT_debug_utils` extension is already integrated in the backend ([#13792](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/13792) added object/pipeline and queue naming), but it does not record command-buffer labels around their corresponding dispatches. I'd like the backend to emit those labels when the existing `GGML_VK_DEBUG_MARKERS` env variable is set, so that any debug_utils-aware profiler (RGP, RenderDoc, Nsight) shows the underlying op name instead of anonymous dispatches. Observed this on master at commit: [ed7adbf](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/ed7adbfefd5e3af5f1c7c04ac67145783def85c5) ### Motivation There is currently no way to tell which op a given dispatch is running when looking at a GPU profiler trace using the Vulkan backend. The existing `GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER` only reports aggregate per-op timings as text, so mapping a bottleneck you see in a profiler back to a specific op has to be done by hand. For example, when I profiled the ROCm/HIP backend, each kernel showed up under its own name in the trace. The Vulkan backend doesn't appear to do that the dispatches don't show per-op naming so you just get anonymous entries. I think this would matter for anyone doing perf work on the Vulkan backend. Since Vulkan is cross-vendor (AMD, Nvidia, Intel), this would help developers across a lot of hardware. Giving dispatches real names in any profiler that uses debug_utils would make it much easier to see where the compute/memory bottlenecks actually are instead of cross-referencing by hand. It also builds on the debug_utils support that's already in the backend. ### Possible Implementation I've already put together a working implementation on my fork, on the branch [vulkan-rgp-debug-labels](https://github.com/CordellBlanchard/llama.cpp/tree/vulkan-rgp-debug-labels). It uses VK_EXT_debug_utils command buffer labels, recording them into the command buffer per dispatch/node. This is done so profilers like RGP (and presumably RenderDoc and Nsight, which I haven't tested) display named regions with the op and tensor name (e.g. MUL_MAT attn_out-19). The regions are opened and closed by a small RAII helper so they stay balanced. In some edge cases I hit while testing, a node can start at the end of one command buffer and finish in the next. So I made it so that any open labels are closed before the buffer ends and reopened on the next one, which keeps each command buffer balanced and renders correctly in the profilers visual timeline. This new change only happens when the existing `GGML_VK_DEBUG_MARKERS` env var is set and is a no-op otherwise so no possible overhead is added on a normal run. Feature Request: Potential unnecessary V-cache allocation for DSA / Lightning Indexer

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

## Potential unnecessary V-cache allocation for DSA / Lightning Indexer

### Description

While investigating the memory usage of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the DSA/Lightning Indexer implementation, I noticed that llama.cpp appears to allocate both K and V storage for the Lightning Indexer cache.

For example, with 12 indexed layers and a context size of 4096, llama.cpp reports:

```text
llama_kv_cache: CUDA0 KV buffer size = 36.00 MiB (indexer KV)

llama_kv_cache: size = 36.00 MiB
(4096 cells, 12 layers, 1/1 seqs),
K (f16): 12.00 MiB,
V (f16): 24.00 MiB
```

However, the corresponding Hugging Face implementation (`DynamicIndexedLayer`) only maintains `indexer_keys`. Its `update_indexer()` method is:

```python
def update_indexer(self, indexer_key_states):
    if not self.is_indexer_initialized:
        self.lazy_initialization_indexer(indexer_key_states)
    self.indexer_keys = torch.cat(
        [self.indexer_keys, indexer_key_states], dim=1
    )
    return self.indexer_keys
```

There is no separate `indexer_values` state.

The llama.cpp DSA implementation also appears to reuse the generic `llama_kv_cache` for the indexer cache, modifying the K dimensions to match the indexer.

This results in:

* Indexer K: 12 MiB
* Indexer V: 24 MiB

The K allocation corresponds to the actual indexer keys, while I'm not currently able to identify a corresponding architectural requirement for the V allocation.

At 8192 tokens, this becomes:

* Indexer K: 24 MiB
* Indexer V: 48 MiB
* Total: 72 MiB

### Question

Is the V buffer in the DSA/Lightning Indexer cache actually required during graph execution, or is it only being allocated because the indexer cache currently uses the generic K/V cache abstraction?

If the V buffer is not required, could the indexer cache be changed to use K-only storage and avoid this additional allocation?

I'm happy to investigate further or work on a PR if this is considered a worthwhile optimization.

### Environment

* Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
* Backend: CUDA
* dtype: F16/BF16
* DSA / Lightning Indexer enabled
* llama.cpp: Latest
* GPU: RTX pro 6000


### Motivation

Removing the unnecessary V allocation would reduce VRAM usage for users running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and potentially other models using similar indexed-attention mechanisms. The saving scales linearly with context length; for example, at 8192 tokens the current indexer allocation would be approximately 72 MiB, of which 48 MiB is the V buffer.

This would be particularly useful for users running large models on GPUs with limited VRAM, where relatively small persistent allocations can determine whether a model/context configuration fits at all.

I am opening this issue first to confirm whether the V buffer is actually required by the current DSA implementation and whether a K-only cache representation would be appropriate.

### Possible Implementation

A possible implementation would be to introduce a K-only cache representation for the Lightning Indexer instead of using the full `llama_kv_cache` abstraction.

Before making this change, the first step would be to verify that the DSA execution path never reads or otherwise requires `kv_lid`'s V buffer. If confirmed, the indexer cache could store only K tensors while retaining the existing interface/behavior required by the DSA implementation.

Conceptually:

    Main attention cache:
        K + V

    Lightning Indexer cache:
        K only

rather than:

    Main attention cache:
        K + V

    Lightning Indexer cache:
        K + V

One possible approach would be to add a lightweight K-only cache class/storage path specifically for DSA, rather than changing the semantics of the existing generic `llama_kv_cache`. This would minimize the risk of affecting models that genuinely require both K and V.

The implementation should preserve the existing tensor dimensions, memory layout, device placement, and cache update behavior for the indexer keys. The main attention KV cache would remain unchanged.


The relevant existing implementation is:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/llama-kv-cache-dsa.cpp

libllama (core library), llama-server

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

An MTP draft context should only allocate KV cache space for the NextN block. Comparing architectures with a DECODER_MTP graph against those create_memory covers, DEEPSEEK2, GLM4_MOE, and COHERE2MOE architectures allocate KV cache space for all layers instead of only NextN layers. All three architectures assert n_layer_nextn == 1 ([src/models/deepseek2.cpp:173](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/models/deepseek2.cpp#L173), [src/models/glm4-moe.cpp:135](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/models/glm4-moe.cpp#L135), [src/models/cohere2moe.cpp:298](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/models/cohere2moe.cpp#L298)) but current allocation is based on n_layer_all instead of n_layer_nextn. This means for a model like GLM-4.6 which has 93 blocks, it is allocating 93x the space actually needed for MTP context. The main context is unfiltered as well, so across both contexts, 2x the needed amount is being allocated and it scales with --ctx-size. With a target GGUF that carries the NextN block: wrong = 2 × n_layer_all; correct = n_layer() +  n_layer_nextn = n_layer_all.


llama_kv_cache allocates one KV pair per layer over n_layer_all, and only skips a layer when it is filtered out. 

         src/llama-kv-cache.cpp:102   const uint32_t n_layer = hparams.n_layer_all;
         src/llama-kv-cache.cpp:171   if (filter && !filter(il)) { ... continue; }

If filter == nullptr, then every layer is allocated.

create_memory never assigns filters for DEEPSEEK2, GLM4_MOE, and COHERE2MOE architectures so all of them fall to default state where filter == nullptr ([src/llama-model.cpp:2610](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/llama-model.cpp#L2610)). 

Only one of these layers is ever addressed. llama_model_deepseek2::graph_mtp has no layer loop ([src/models/deepseek2.cpp:178](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/models/deepseek2.cpp#L178)):

And n_layer() = n_layer_all - n_layer_nextn ([src/llama-hparams.cpp:347-349](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/74a7c897f049c17e7080423aa2111776eff6ebbf/src/llama-hparams.cpp#L347-L349)), so il >= n_layer() selects exactly the NextN blocks.

            hparams.n_layer_nextn > 0) {

### Name and Version

commit 96ffdc41c (master, 2026-09-14), built locally with -DGGML_VULKAN=ON, GNU 16.2.1, Linux x86_64
ggml_vulkan: 0 = AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT (RADV GFX1201) (radv) | uma: 0 | fp16: dot2 | bf16: 1 | fp4: 0 | warp size: 64 | shared memory: 65536 | int dot: 1 | matrix cores: KHR_coopmat

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell
VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS=VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation VK_LAYER_GPUAV_ENABLE=1 \
  ./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -b Vulkan0 -o IM2COL
# same for -o IM2COL_3D
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Affected module: ggml-vulkan, the `im2col` and `im2col_3d` compute shaders.
 
Both shaders declare their output pointer type with `buffer_reference` but no `buffer_reference_align`. Without it, glslang emits every `OpStore` through that pointer with `Aligned 16`, but the shaders advance the pointer by `D_SIZE` (4 bytes for f32, 2 for f16), so most writes land on addresses that aren't 16-byte aligned. Under the PhysicalStorageBuffer64 addressing model the spec requires the pointer to be at least as aligned as the `Aligned` operand says, so this is undefined behavior. RADV happens to produce correct results today, which is why tests pass, but another driver (or a future RADV) is free to miscompile or fault on it.
 
Found by running `test-backend-ops` with Vulkan validation layers and GPU-AV enabled.
 
Declarations:
- `ggml/src/ggml-vulkan/vulkan-shaders/im2col.comp:34`
- `ggml/src/ggml-vulkan/vulkan-shaders/im2col_3d.comp:53`
```glsl
  layout (buffer_reference) buffer D_ptr {D_TYPE d;};
```
- Writes: `D_ptr(current_dst_addr).d = D_TYPE(val);` with `current_dst_addr += bda_step;` where `bda_step = D_SIZE * BLOCK_SIZE` and `D_SIZE` is 4 (f32) or 2 (f16), see `vulkan-shaders-gen.cpp:1109-1110`
- VUID: `VUID-RuntimeSpirv-PhysicalStorageBuffer64-06315`

| op | as is | with `buffer_reference_align = D_SIZE` |
|---|---|---|
| IM2COL | 92/92 tests passed, 06315 reported | 92/92 tests passed, 0 validation messages |
| IM2COL_3D | 2051/2051 tests passed, 06315 reported | 2051/2051 tests passed, 0 validation messages |
 
Candidate change (both files):
```diff
-layout (buffer_reference) buffer D_ptr {D_TYPE d;};
+layout (buffer_reference, buffer_reference_align = D_SIZE) buffer D_ptr {D_TYPE d;};
```
 
This only tells the compiler the real alignment of the pointer, so it shouldn't change results on drivers that already behave. I'm happy to open the PR with this change if it looks right.

d8359f5fde  vulkan: 64-bit im2col (#16135)

### Relevant log output

<summary>Logs</summary>


```console
Validation Error: [ VUID-RuntimeSpirv-PhysicalStorageBuffer64-06315 ] | MessageID = 0x74774701
vkCmdDispatch(): Unaligned pointer access: The OpStore at buffer device address 0xffff8001045e3304 is not aligned to the instruction Aligned operand of 16.
Address belongs to the follwing buffer(s):

Stage = Compute.  Global invocation ID (x, y, z) = (1, 365, 0)
Command buffer (0x5589bab1c900)

SPIR-V Instruction: OpStore %572 %650 2 16
The Vulkan spec states: If the PhysicalStorageBuffer64 addressing model is enabled the pointer value of a memory access instruction must be at least as aligned as specified by the Aligned memory access operand
```

query:
ggml-backend: discarded ggml_gallocr_reserve_n return value turns an allocation failure into a segfault

### Summary

`ggml_backend_sched_alloc_splits` discards the return value of `ggml_gallocr_reserve_n`. When the reserve fails because a CUDA allocation failed, the allocator is left partial, `ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph` then runs against it, and the process segfaults instead of returning an error through the path that already exists.

The same call is checked at `ggml-backend.cpp:1929`. It is only the site at line 1586 that drops it.

### Where

`ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp:1586`

```c
ggml_gallocr_reserve_n(sched->galloc, &sched->graph, sched->node_backend_ids, sched->leaf_backend_ids);
if (!ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph(sched->galloc, &sched->graph)) {
    GGML_LOG_ERROR("%s: failed to allocate graph\n", __func__);
    return false;
}
```

`ggml_gallocr_reserve_n` is declared `bool` and documented at `ggml-alloc.h:64` to return false when the buffer allocation fails.

### What I see

Running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (PR #27742, `qwen4exp`) on 2x RTX 3090 with the routed experts split between the two cards and host RAM. The server loads, answers short prompts correctly, then dies partway through a long prompt. The allocation failure is reported, so the cause is visible, and then the process goes down with no further output:

```
prompt processing, n_tokens = 17849, progress = 0.90, t = 36.54 s / 488.50 tokens per second
ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 1599.01 MiB on device 1: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
ggml_gallocr_reserve_n_impl: failed to allocate CUDA1 buffer of size 1676685440
Segmentation fault
```

Reproduced three times, at 17849, 26624 and 59392 tokens, across two different expert placements and at both `-ub 2048` and `-ub 1024`.

### Proposed fix

Untested beyond reading the surrounding code, so treat it as a proposal rather than a patch I have run:

```diff
-    ggml_gallocr_reserve_n(sched->galloc, &sched->graph, sched->node_backend_ids, sched->leaf_backend_ids);
+    if (!ggml_gallocr_reserve_n(sched->galloc, &sched->graph, sched->node_backend_ids, sched->leaf_backend_ids)) {
+        GGML_LOG_ERROR("%s: failed to reserve graph\n", __func__);
+        return false;
+    }
     if (!ggml_gallocr_alloc_graph(sched->galloc, &sched->graph)) {
         GGML_LOG_ERROR("%s: failed to allocate graph\n", __func__);
         return false;
     }
```

That routes into the handled path: false becomes `GGML_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED`, then -2 from `llama_decode`, then the server's `Compute error.` branch, which releases the slots and reports the failure rather than taking the process down. Happy to open a PR once someone confirms the approach is what you want.

### Why this architecture reaches it easily

The failure is generic, but `qwen4exp` makes it easy to hit. Its sparse attention bias input is sized `[n_kv, n_tps, n_stream]`, so the compute buffer grows with the prompt length actually processed rather than with `-c`. Fitting the three failures above gives roughly 971 MiB fixed plus 1.8e-5 MiB per token times ubatch, which reproduces all three within 130 MiB across a 3.3x span of prompt lengths and a 2x span of ubatch. So a configuration that loads cleanly and serves short prompts can still run out on a long one, at which point you get a segfault rather than an error.

### Repro

2x RTX 3090, 24 GiB each, 54 GiB host RAM, no swap. Build from PR #27742 at `6c5afc8`, CUDA 13.0.2, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86`.

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -sm layer -fit off -c 32768 -fa on -ctk f16 -ctv f16 \
  -b 2048 -ub 2048 -t 8 \
  -ot "^per_layer_token_embd\.weight$=CPU" \
  -ot "blk\.([0-8]|2[5-9]|3[01])\.ffn_(up|down|gate|gate_up)_(ch|)exps=CPU"
```

Then send a prompt of roughly 18,000 tokens.

### Name and Version

`llama-server` built from `unslothai/llama.cpp` branch `qwen4exp/qwen3.8-flash-next` at `6c5afc8` (PR #27742), CUDA build, Ubuntu 24.04, driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.0.88.

The fix mirrors the existing check at line 1929, wrapping the `ggml_gallocr_reserve_n` call at line 1586 in an `if (!...)` guard so the failure propagates as `GGML_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED` rather than segfaulting downstream.

Its top is ``` root ::= start message* scan-to-toolcall tool-call message ::= (thought | ) content content ::= until-165 # until one of <|channel> / / <|tool_call> scan-to-toolcall ::= until-162 # until <|tool_call> tool-call ::= ("<|tool_call>call:" (tool-extract-soul-data) "") ``` and every `until-N` rule is compiled as a chain in which each partial-delimiter state has an empty alternative: ``` until-165 ::= | [<] until-165-01 | [^<] until-165 until-165-01 ::= | [<] until-165-01 | [|] until-165-02 | [c] until-165-11 | [^] until-165 # after "<|tool_call": ">" excluded ``` Results (`valid` = accepted as complete; `incomplete` = accepted as a prefix, "Unexpected end of input"; `INVALID` = rejected): | input | result | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | `<\|tool_call>call:extract_soul_data{a:<\|"\|>x<\|"\|>}` | valid | | `<\|tool_call>call:extract_soul_data{a:<\|"\|>x<\|"\|>]}` | incomplete | | `<\|tool_call>call:extract_soul_data{a:<\|"\|>x<\|"\|>ZZZ` | incomplete | | `<\|tool_call>call:extract_soul_data{a:<\|"\|>x<\|"\|>}ZZZ` | incomplete | | `anything ] } { <\|tool_call>call:nope{` + the valid call | **valid** | | the valid call twice | **valid** | The second, third and fourth rows should be `INVALID` at the first bad byte; instead every byte is accepted. The last two rows say why: the grammar has a live parse in which `content` consumes `<|tool_call` (stopping before the `>` it may not take), and `scan-to-toolcall`, a fresh `until`, then consumes `>call:…` and everything after it as plain scan text, waiting for a _later_ `<|tool_call>`. The delimiter is split across two adjacent `until` rules. Because llama.cpp's grammar sampler constrains the next token by the union of all live stacks, that stack alone makes any byte legal for the rest of the generation, the dict/array/string rules only ever bite if the model happens to emit a second `<|tool_call>`. So for this format, `tool_choice: required` produces a grammar that is effectively unconstrained once the call begins. On device (Gemma 4 E2B, Q4 QAT) we see the consequence as roughly one extraction in 15–25 with a structurally impossible token in it (`]` for `}`, an unclosed string, a doubled key), all rejected by the PEG parse, all with the raw text accepted as a prefix by the grammar. ### Where I think the fix goes The `until` compilation needs its partial-delimiter states to be non-final, the empty alternative should exist only at `until-N` itself (before any delimiter byte has been consumed), not at `until-N-01…28`. Equivalently: an `until(d)` must not be able to end with a proper prefix of `d` consumed. With that, `content` cannot stop after `<|tool_call` and the only way past a `<|tool_call>` is the `tool-call` rule. I'm happy to test a patch against the same inputs; the validator makes it a five-second check.

Misc. bug: server: (router) --api-key is not forwarded to child instances while --api-key-file is

### Name and Version

 version: 0.4.0-dev (build 158, commit 311d4211b)

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama serve --port 8080 --models-preset corral-preset.ini --api-key 6614372 --api-key-file keys.txt（use 123 and 234)
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

In router mode, --api-key and --api-key-file are supposed to be the same kind of key source (both just add keys to   
 the accepted list), but they are not treated the same when the router spawns child model instances.                    
                                                                                                                        
   What I see:                                                                                                          
   - GET /v1/models accepts all keys (router, 6614372 / 123 / 234 all return 200)                                       
   - POST /v1/chat/completions (proxied to the child) accepts only the file keys (123/234 -> 200), the CLI key 6614372  
 -> 401 "Invalid API Key"                                                                                               
   - ps on the spawned child shows --api-key-file in its args but no --api-key                                          
                                                                                                                        
   So a client that authenticates with the CLI key can list models but cannot use the server at all. I hit this from a  
 real client (chat requests all 401) while the server looked healthy.                                                   
                                                                                                                        
   Root cause I found: in tools/server/server-models.cpp, unset_reserved_args(base_preset, true) runs before            
 preset.merge(base_preset), and it unsets LLAMA_API_KEY. LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY_FILE is not in the reserved list, so only    
 the file source survives to the child's args. The child then validates against file keys only.                         
                                                                                                                        
   This looks like it has been there since the preset refactor #18169. Related but distinct (already fixed): #24763     
 restored the base_preset merge pass itself.                                                                            
                                                                                                                        
   Suggested fix: stop unsetting LLAMA_API_KEY (children listening on router-assigned loopback ports re-validating the  
 same key union is harmless), or at least forward both sources consistently. A test asserting "every key the router     
 accepts is also accepted by a spawned child" would catch this.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. The unset of LLAMA_API_KEY in unset_reserved_args() has been there since the preset refactor (#18169); 
 the forwarding mechanism itself was broken separately and fixed in #24763.

### Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>


```console

```
</details>
hints:
Correction to the command line above (stray note mixed in):                                                          
                                                                                                                        
   llama serve --port 8080 --models-preset corral-preset.ini --api-key 6614372 --api-key-file keys.txt                  
                                                                                                                        
   keys.txt contains two lines: 123 and 234

I think the fix should go the other way around. Rather than forwarding --api-key to the children, we should also stop forwarding --api-key-file, so that no key ever reaches a child. Authentication belongs to the router, children only listen on loopback on a router assigned port, and the proxy already forwards the Authorization header untouched, so every key the router accepts keeps working end to end. It also keeps the secret out of the child argv. And it fixes a second problem along the way, since the router calls POST /v1/streams/lookup and DELETE /v1/stream on the child without an Authorization header, which means those calls silently 401 today whenever --api-key-file is used.

Dear Team,

I would like to report a successful resolution of a severe memory-related stability issue encountered while running the Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_XL GGUF model with llama.cpp and the Intel SYCL backend on an Intel Arc A770.

The initial configuration consistently resulted in GPU memory allocation failures and, in some cases, system-level memory pressure severe enough to trigger process termination. The investigation showed that the problem was not caused by VMM, Level Zero, ESIMD, or fusion support, as initially suspected.

We isolated the issue by testing the SYCL features independently. The decisive finding was that:

* `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_HOST_PINNED_MEM=1` causes the crash in our environment.
* `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_HOST_PINNED_MEM=0` provides stable execution.
* `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=1` works correctly.
* `GGML_SYCL_USE_LEVEL_ZERO_API=1` works correctly.
* `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_FUSION=1` works correctly.
* `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_ESIMD=1` works correctly.

An additional issue was identified with the batch configuration. Using `--batch-size 1` resulted in the assertion:

`GGML_ASSERT(n_tokens_all <= cparams.n_batch)`

Increasing the configuration to:

`--batch-size 32`
`--ubatch-size 32`

resolved this problem.

With these findings, the stable single-GPU configuration became:

`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=1`
`GGML_SYCL_USE_LEVEL_ZERO_API=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_FUSION=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_ESIMD=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_HOST_PINNED_MEM=0`

Using the Intel Arc A770 alone, we were able to offload 30 layers of the 66-layer model and obtain approximately:

* Prompt processing: 15.5 tokens/s
* Generation: 5.8 tokens/s

The decisive step was then to use both Intel GPUs in layer-split mode:

`--device SYCL0,SYCL1`
`--split-mode layer`
`--n-gpu-layers 66`

with:

* SYCL0: Intel Arc Pro B50 16 GB
* SYCL1: Intel Arc A770 16 GB

This configuration successfully offloaded all 66/66 layers:

* B50 model buffer: approximately 7.65 GiB
* A770 model buffer: approximately 8.07 GiB
* CPU-mapped model buffer: only approximately 682 MiB

The model therefore became effectively GPU-resident across the two cards, avoiding the excessive system RAM consumption that previously caused Chrome and other desktop applications to be terminated by memory reclaim.

Most importantly, the system is now fully functional end-to-end. The Qwen3.8-27B model loads successfully, the SYCL/Level Zero execution path is stable, and inference completes correctly.

With the dual-GPU configuration we measured:

* Prompt processing: approximately 17.2 tokens/s
* Generation: approximately 11.8 tokens/s

This represents roughly a 2× improvement in generation throughput compared with the previous A770-only configuration using 30 GPU layers.

The final stable configuration is therefore:

`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_VMM=1`
`GGML_SYCL_USE_LEVEL_ZERO_API=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_FUSION=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_ESIMD=1`
`GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_HOST_PINNED_MEM=0`

combined with:

`--device SYCL0,SYCL1`
`--split-mode layer`
`--n-gpu-layers 66`
`--ctx-size 2048`
`--batch-size 32`
`--ubatch-size 32`
`--flash-attn off`
`--fit off`
`--no-warmup`

In summary, the issue was resolved without disabling the SYCL features that were originally suspected to be responsible. The key requirement was to disable Host Pinned Memory explicitly and to use an appropriate batch size. Once this was done, the model could be distributed across the B50 and A770, achieving full 66-layer GPU offload with dramatically reduced system RAM usage and significantly higher inference throughput.

I believe this is a useful data point for investigating the interaction between llama.cpp, the Intel SYCL/Level Zero stack, and mixed Intel GPU architectures (BMG + DG2), particularly with Qwen35/Qwen3.8 models using Gated Delta Net and related fused operations.

Eval bug: tick() evicts models which are being requested -> requests fail due to http client error

### Name and Version

marco@marco-desktop:~/ai/llama.cpp/build/bin$ ./llama-cli --version
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10867, commit f3f1a8f27)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

HIP

### Hardware

i5-9600k + RX 9070 XT

### Models

In this case, I reproduced with the following models, but I think it will work with any models:
- Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-Q4_K_M - https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-14B-Reasoning-2512-GGUF
- gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K (https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-GGUF)
- Spark-X2.5-1.7B-Q8_0 (https://huggingface.co/XHToken/Spark-X2.5-1.7B-GGUF)
- Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0 (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B-GGUF)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

To fix #28443 , a `tick()` function was introduced to help evict models more reliably. But it seems that it is a bit too trigger happy. 

When using llama-server in router mode with `--models-max 1`, I have found that the tick() function will evict models which are currently being requested. This request will then be routed into nothingness with the following error message in the llama.cpp log:
`operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`

I have also tested this issue with the code from PR #28555 (commit 87273462b), which unfortunately did not fix the problem either.

I'm running llama.cpp in router mode using the following command:
`./llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server --models-preset "/home/marco/ai/llm/models.ini" --port 9553 --models-max 1`

I have tried to find the exact conditions to reproduce the issue. There seems to be two failure modes:
- **Variant A:** If no model is loaded and the server is hit with two simultaneous requests, one model gets evicted before it can fulfil the request. We get `operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`.
- **Variant B:** If model A is loaded, a request comes in for a different model B will trigger unload. If during unload, another request comes in for model A, which is in the process of unloading, that request for model A will never be served. We get `operator(): got exception: {"error":{"code":500,"message":"request cancelled while waiting for model name=gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K","type":"server_error"}}` with subsequent `operator(): http client error: Could not establish connection`.

Find below a bash script that will reproduce the issue every time on my machine. I have attached logs for variants A and B into the relevant log output section of this issue. Disclaimer: Script has been AI generated by GLM-5.3.

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# repro.sh - llama.cpp router eviction race, two variants
#
# Variant A: ./repro.sh a
#   The request that loads a model through the fast path (slot free, queue
#   empty) has its model evicted the moment it reports LOADED, before the
#   request reaches proxy_request() and increments req_count.
#
# Variant B: ./repro.sh b
#   A queued request for another model evicts an idle loaded model. A new
#   request for that same model arrives while the child is still shutting
#   down; admission still sees LOADED and proxies into the dying child.
#
# Requirements:
#   - llama-server in router mode, --models-max 1
#   - jq
#   - no other traffic while the script runs
#     (an idle Open WebUI is fine, it only fires requests when you use it)
#
# Both variants reset the router first (POST /models/unload for everything
# loaded), so no restart is needed between runs.

set -u

ROUTER="${ROUTER:-http://127.0.0.1:9553}"
MODEL_A="${MODEL_A:-gemma-4-12b-it-Q6_K}"           # victim, must load slow (see variant b)
MODEL_B_A="${MODEL_B_A:-Qwen3-Embedding-4B-Q8_0}"   # variant A: any other model
MODEL_B_B="${MODEL_B_B:-Spark-X2.5-1.7B-Q8_0}"      # variant B: any other model
DELAY="${DELAY:-0.03}"                              # variant B: gap between the queued
                                                    # request and the new victim request

command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "this script needs jq" >&2; exit 1; }

chat() { # chat <model> <outfile> [max-time]
  if [ -n "${3:-}" ]; then
    curl -s --max-time "$3" "$ROUTER/v1/chat/completions" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hi\"}]}" > "$2"
  else
    curl -s "$ROUTER/v1/chat/completions" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"hi\"}]}" > "$2"
  fi
}

embed() { # embed <model> <outfile>
  curl -s "$ROUTER/v1/embeddings" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"model\":\"$1\",\"input\":\"hi\"}" > "$2"
}

status_of() { # status_of <model>
  curl -s "$ROUTER/models" | jq -r --arg m "$1" '.data[] | select(.id==$m) | .status.value'
}

loaded_models() {
  curl -s "$ROUTER/models" | jq -r \
    '.data[] | select(.status.value=="loaded" or .status.value=="loading" or .status.value=="sleeping") | .id'
}

reset_router() { # make the router cold: nothing loaded, queue empty
  local m
  for m in $(loaded_models); do
    curl -s -X POST "$ROUTER/models/unload" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d "{\"model\":\"$m\"}" > /dev/null
  done
  local i=0
  while [ -n "$(loaded_models)" ]; do
    sleep 0.5
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ $i -gt 60 ]; then
      echo "router did not go idle, check $ROUTER/models" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

wait_loaded() { # wait_loaded <model>
  local i=0
  while [ "$(status_of "$1")" != "loaded" ]; do
    sleep 0.5
    i=$((i+1))
    if [ $i -gt 180 ]; then
      echo "timeout waiting for $1 to be loaded" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

variant_a() {
  echo "== variant A: fast path load evicted at the LOADED transition =="
  reset_router || return 1

  echo "1. chat request for $MODEL_A (fast path: slot free, queue empty)"
  chat "$MODEL_A" /tmp/repro_a_chat.json &

  sleep 0.5   # stay inside the load window of MODEL_A

  echo "2. embeddings request for $MODEL_B_A joins the queue"
  embed "$MODEL_B_A" /tmp/repro_a_embed.json &

  wait
  echo
  echo "chat request for $MODEL_A answered:"
  cat /tmp/repro_a_chat.json; echo
  echo
  if grep -q "proxy error" /tmp/repro_a_chat.json; then
    echo "REPRODUCED: the request that loaded $MODEL_A was proxied into its own eviction"
  else
    echo "NOT reproduced, $MODEL_A was served normally."
    echo "Was the router idle before the run? A queued request protects a load."
  fi
}

variant_b() {
  echo "== variant B: idle model evicted, new request for it lands in the stop window =="
  reset_router || return 1

  echo "1. orphan $MODEL_A: client cancelled while the model still loads"
  # MODEL_A must load slower than 2 s here, else the request completes and the
  # model goes idle after serving (that also works, but the timing gets fuzzy)
  chat "$MODEL_A" /tmp/repro_b_cancel.json 2
  wait_loaded "$MODEL_A" || return 1
  echo "   $MODEL_A is now loaded and idle, no request behind it"
  # same idle state without the cancel:
  #   curl -s -X POST "$ROUTER/models/load" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  #        -d "{\"model\":\"$MODEL_A\"}" > /dev/null && wait_loaded "$MODEL_A"

  echo "2. chat request for $MODEL_B_B queues and evicts idle $MODEL_A"
  chat "$MODEL_B_B" /tmp/repro_b_b.json &

  echo "3. new chat request for $MODEL_A after ${DELAY}s"
  sleep "$DELAY"
  chat "$MODEL_A" /tmp/repro_b_new.json &

  wait
  echo
  echo "new request for $MODEL_A answered:"
  cat /tmp/repro_b_new.json; echo
  echo
  if grep -q "proxy error" /tmp/repro_b_new.json; then
    echo "REPRODUCED: the new $MODEL_A request was proxied into the dying child"
  else
    echo "NOT reproduced, the request missed the stop window."
    echo "Sweep the delay:"
    echo "  for d in 0.01 0.02 0.05 0.08 0.12; do DELAY=\$d ./repro.sh b; done"
    echo "The window runs from the eviction to the moment the router notices"
    echo "the child exit, roughly 10 to 150 ms on my machine."
  fi
}

case "${1:-}" in
  a)      variant_a ;;
  b)      variant_b ;;
  status) curl -s "$ROUTER/models" | jq '.data[] | {id: .id, status: .status.value}' ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: $0 a|b|status"
    echo "  a        variant A, fast path load evicted at the LOADED transition"
    echo "  b        variant B, idle model evicted, new request hits the stop window"
    echo "  status   list models and their status"
    echo "env: ROUTER, MODEL_A, MODEL_B_A, MODEL_B_B, DELAY (variant b)"
    ;;
esac
```

Eval bug: SIGSEGV in token-counting routes when the request arrives while the server is sleeping (stale vocab/mctx captured before the wake barrier)

### Name and Version

version: 0.4.0-dev
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64, GGML_CUDA=ON, Release

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

Router parent:

```
llama-server --host 127.0.0.1 --port PORT --models-preset models.ini \
  --models-max 1 --no-models-autoload --api-key-file KEYFILE --no-webui
```

Children are spawned by the router from the preset with:

```
--sleep-idle-seconds 300 --ctx-size 65536 --batch-size 256 --ubatch-size 128 \
--flash-attn on --n-gpu-layers auto --parallel 1 --reasoning off \
--fit-target 2048 --no-warmup --no-webui --mmproj MMPROJ --no-mmproj-offload \
--image-min-tokens N
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Send a single request to any of the token-counting routes to a child that has
gone to sleep via `--sleep-idle-seconds`. The server segfaults.

Reproduced deliberately: one child idle for ~4h18m, one POST to
`/v1/chat/completions/input_tokens`, immediate SIGSEGV. Eight core dumps so far,
all on the same path, every one of them after a wake from idle sleep, never on a
cold start. No concurrency required — a single request is sufficient.

Affected routes (three handler lambdas, five registered URLs):

```
/chat/completions/input_tokens
/v1/chat/completions/input_tokens
/responses/input_tokens
/v1/responses/input_tokens
/v1/messages/count_tokens
```

`/tokenize`, `/detokenize` and ordinary `/v1/chat/completions` are NOT affected.

### Cause

`tools/server/server-context.cpp` states the invariant at the top of
`init_routes()`:

```cpp
// IMPORTANT: all lambda functions must start with create_response()
// this is to ensure that the server_res_generator can handle sleeping case correctly
```

`create_response()` constructs `server_res_generator`, which calls
`queue_tasks.wait_until_no_sleep()` — the wake barrier.

Every route lambda obeys this except the three that call `handle_count_tokens`,
which evaluate `ctx_server.vocab` and `ctx_server.mctx` as call arguments
*before* the callee reaches its own `create_response()`:

```cpp
this->post_chat_completions_tok = [this](const server_http_req & req) {
    return handle_count_tokens(ctx_server.vocab, ctx_server.mctx, ctx_server.init_opt, req, TASK_RESPONSE_TYPE_OAI_CHAT);
};
```

(same shape for `post_responses_tok_oai` and `post_anthropic_count_tokens`)

While sleeping, `destroy()` has torn the model down:

```cpp
void destroy() {
    spec.reset();
    spec_init.reset();
    ctx_dft   = nullptr;
    model_dft = nullptr;
    llama_init.reset();
    ctx_tgt   = nullptr;
    model_tgt = nullptr;
    mtmd_free(mctx);
    mctx = nullptr;
}
```

So the arguments captured at call time are a stale `vocab` (pointing into the
freed model) and a null `mctx`. `handle_count_tokens` then calls
`create_response()`, which waits for the wake; the reload installs a fresh
`vocab` on the member via `llama_model_get_vocab(model_tgt)` — but the copies
already passed as arguments are never refreshed. The null-`mctx` branch then
runs `tokenize_mixed(vocab, ...)` through the stale pointer.

Note this is an ordering bug, not a missing-reset bug: nulling `vocab` in
`destroy()` would not fix it, because the member is legitimately reassigned on
reload. The captured argument is the problem.

### Suggested fix

Read `ctx_server.vocab` / `ctx_server.mctx` / `ctx_server.init_opt` inside
`handle_count_tokens` *after* `create_response()` returns, rather than passing
them in — or pass `ctx_server` by reference and dereference post-barrier.

### Relevant context

`destroy()` has been corrected once before for omitted teardown (#23461). The
sleep feature also already shipped one use-after-free fix for a chat-template
pointer (#18228, commit 105e2f3). This looks like the same class, one pointer
further on.

In router mode the parent forwards the request straight through to the sleeping
child by design — `ensure_model_ready()` returns early on
`SERVER_MODEL_STATUS_SLEEPING` with the comment "child is sleeping but still
running; new request will wake it up" — so any router client whose first call of
a turn is a token count will hit this every time.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. The token-counting routes were introduced in #23913.

### Relevant log output

```
SIGSEGV, si_code: SEGV_MAPERR
top frame, 5 of 8 cores:  llama_vocab::impl::tokenize
top frame, 3 of 8 cores:  llama_vocab::impl::tokenizer_st_partition
reached from server_routes::handle_count_tokens
```

- `post_anthropic_count_tokens` → `/v1/messages/count_tokens`

**Why it crashes:** these lambdas evaluate `ctx_server.vocab`, `ctx_server.mctx` and `ctx_server.init_opt` as call arguments *before* `handle_count_tokens` reaches `create_response()`, which is the wake barrier (`wait_until_no_sleep()`). While the server is asleep, `destroy()` has freed the model and set `mctx = nullptr`, so the captured `vocab` is stale. The reload assigns a fresh `vocab` to the member, but the copies already passed in are never refreshed, and the null-`mctx` branch then tokenizes through the stale pointer.

**Suggested fix:** read `vocab` / `mctx` / `init_opt` from `ctx_server` *inside* `handle_count_tokens`, after `create_response()` returns. Or pass `ctx_server` by reference and dereference it after the barrier. Nulling `vocab` in `destroy()` would not help, because the member is legitimately reassigned on reload.

**Reproduce:**
1. Start `llama-server` with `--sleep-idle-seconds` set (I used 300; a short value should behave the same, but I only reproduced it after a long idle).
2. Wait for it to go to sleep.
3. Send a single POST to `/v1/chat/completions/input_tokens`. It segfaults right away.

No concurrency is needed. `/tokenize`, `/detokenize` and a normal `/v1/chat/completions` are not affected, because they go through `create_response()` first. A regression test in `tools/server/tests` would do sleep → count_tokens → assert 200.

**Evidence:** 8 cores, all `SIGSEGV`/`SEGV_MAPERR`, every one after a wake from idle sleep and never on a cold start. The top frame was `llama_vocab::impl::tokenize` in 5 of them and `llama_vocab::impl::tokenizer_st_partition` in 3, reached from `server_routes::handle_count_tokens`.

Related: #18228 (earlier use-after-free in the sleep path, commit 105e2f3), #23461 (`destroy()` teardown), and #23913 (where these routes were added).

HIP build fails on ROCm 6.2.x — `vendors/hip.h` typedefs `__hip_fp8_e4m3`, which does not exist before ROCm 6.3.0

### Summary

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h` enables the FP8 include and typedef at `HIP_VERSION >= 60200000`,
but the OCP-named type `__hip_fp8_e4m3` first ships in ROCm **6.3.0**. On ROCm 6.2.x only the
FNUZ-named types exist, so the typedef names a type that is not declared and the HIP build fails.

`ggml/src/ggml-hip/CMakeLists.txt` declares `"At least ROCM/HIP V6.1 is required"`, so ROCm 6.2.4 is
inside the supported range.

### Reproduction

Host: ROCm **6.2.4-139**, 5× Radeon VII (gfx906 / Vega20), Ubuntu. llama.cpp master `25ae3a9`.

```
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx906 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j
```

```
/path/to/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h:249:9: error: unknown type name '__hip_fp8_e4m3'
```

This is the only error emitted; the build stops there.

### Offending lines

`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/vendors/hip.h`:

```cpp
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
#include <hip/hip_fp8.h>
typedef __hip_fp8_e4m3 __nv_fp8_e4m3;   // <-- not declared before ROCm 6.3.0
#define FP8_AVAILABLE
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
```

### Header evidence

Local install:

```
$ grep -oE "__hip_fp8_e4m3(_fnuz)?" /opt/rocm/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h | sort -u
__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz

$ grep -c HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP /opt/rocm/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h
0
```

Only the FNUZ name is present, and `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` is not defined at all on this release.

Upstream `ROCm/clr`, `hipamd/include/hip/amd_detail/amd_hip_fp8.h`, at release tags:

| tag | `__hip_fp8_e4m3` (OCP name) | `__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz` | `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rocm-6.2.0` | **not declared** | declared | not defined |
| `rocm-6.2.4` | **not declared** | declared | not defined |
| `rocm-6.3.0` | declared | declared | defined |

The type is absent in both the `rocm-6.2.0` and `rocm-6.2.4` release headers and present in
`rocm-6.3.0`.

### Patch

Keep `FP8_AVAILABLE` at the 6.2 gate; move only the typedef to 6.3:

```cpp
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60200000
#include <hip/hip_fp8.h>
#define FP8_AVAILABLE
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60200000

// The OCP-named FP8 types first ship in ROCm 6.3.0; 6.2.x provides only the *_fnuz names.
#if HIP_VERSION >= 60300000
typedef __hip_fp8_e4m3 __nv_fp8_e4m3;
#endif // HIP_VERSION >= 60300000
```

With only that change, the same tree builds cleanly and runs:

```
$ cmake --build build --target llama-server -j4      # rc=0
$ ./build/bin/llama-server --version
version: 0.1.1-dev (build 1, commit 25ae3a9) built with GNU 13.4.0 for Linux x86_64

$ ./build/bin/test-backend-ops test -o MUL_MAT_ID     # gfx906
869/869 tests passed
```

### Why this shape

- **`FP8_AVAILABLE` stays at the 6.2 gate.** `common.cuh:841` gates the CDNA3 hardware FP8 path on
  `defined(FP8_AVAILABLE) && HIP_VERSION >= 60200000`. Moving the whole block to 6.3 would also fix
  the build but would cost gfx942 that path on ROCm 6.2.x.

- **No FNUZ compatibility alias.** Leaving `__nv_fp8_e4m3` undeclared below 6.3 compiles because
  nothing reachable on HIP uses it: the only two references are `common.cuh:850`, gated
  `defined(FP8_AVAILABLE) && !defined(GGML_USE_HIP)`, and `common.cuh:874`, gated
  `BLACKWELL_MMA_AVAILABLE`. The HIP consumer at `common.cuh:845` names `__hip_fp8_e4m3_fnuz`
  directly. Aliasing FNUZ to the OCP name would also build, but the two are different formats
  (different exponent bias, no infinities in FNUZ), so an alias would be a hazard for future code.

- **Not a `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP` feature test.** That macro looks like the natural guard but answers a
  different question. In the `rocm-6.3.0` header the `__hip_fp8_e4m3` struct declaration is
  controlled independently of `HIP_FP8_TYPE_OCP`; that macro selects target-specific OCP behaviour
  rather than serving as a type-presence test, and it is **0 on gfx942** where the type is
  nonetheless declared. It is also not defined at all on 6.2.x. Type presence here tracks the
  release; the macro tracks the target.

This is a suggested fix rather than a settled one — happy to open a PR, or to take a different
shape if maintainers prefer one.

Eval bug: test-save-load-state aborts on hrm_text with GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC (input-layer tensor makes the backend assignment depend on batch size)

### Name and Version

version: b11194-5-g86a24a182 (master 86a24a182)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA, HIP, Vulkan

### Hardware

RTX 4070 (local).
ggml-ci: T4, ROCm, Intel PTL, Apple.

### Models

`hrm_text-dense.gguf` from `test-generate-models` (any `LLM_ARCH_HRM_TEXT` model).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Test 9 added by #27530 exposes an existing HRM-Text issue under `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC`: `test-save-load-state` aborts on `hrm_text-dense.gguf` in several GPU ctest jobs of ggml-ci (CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan on Intel Linux / NVIDIA / Apple) with `unexpected graph reallocation` (for example: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/actions/runs/36226612703/job/108361769531#step:3:1272). The CPU job passes.

The failure is not in the restore path itself. Test 9 first decodes 8 tokens to obtain the baseline, clears memory, and then decodes 24 tokens. The abort occurs during this second `llama_decode()` (`tests/test-save-load-state.cpp:721`), before any corrupted state is restored.

Cause: `hrm.z_l_init` is registered as `LLM_TENSOR_LAYER_INPUT` (`src/llama-arch.cpp`), so it lives in host memory. The `ggml_add()` with the embeddings in `src/models/hrm-text.cpp` therefore goes through the scheduler's offload rule and is assigned to the GPU only for batches >= 32 rows. The reserve graph (100 tokens) puts it on the GPU, small decodes put it on the CPU, so the allocator is re-reserved for the 8-token graph and the 24-token decode needs another reallocation (`ggml_gallocr_needs_realloc: node embd is not valid`), which `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC` turns into the abort. Without that option it only costs an extra reallocation.

`LLM_TENSOR_TOKEN_EMBD_NORM` avoids the same problem by being placed on the first layer instead of the input layer; doing the same for `hrm.z_l_init` (`LLM_TENSOR_LAYER_REPEATING`, bid 0) makes `test-save-load-state --models` pass 127/127 on CUDA and CPU with `GGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC=ON`.

Repro: build with `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_SCHED_NO_REALLOC=ON`, then `test-save-load-state -m tests/test-models/hrm_text-dense.gguf`.

08618ff8e (#27530) exposes it by adding test 9; the placement dates from 7d6f5d02b (#27625).

version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11188, commit e85e15cf6)
built with GNU 15.1.1 for Linux aarch64

Linux

Test code

```shell
./test-backend-ops -o 'ARGSORT(type=f32,ne=[2048,1,1,1],order=0)'
```

  - `maxComputeWorkGroupInvocations` is `2048`
  -  `maxComputeWorkGroupSize`: `[1024, 1024, 1024]`
- `use_small` is `true` in  `ggml_vk_argsort()`
- `pipeline_argsort_f32[10]` is used, which has `BLOCK_SIZE` of `1024`
- 2 workgroups are dispatched
- Only half of the array is sorted
- Test fails

I think the 2 workgroups end up sorting the first 1024 elements (so those end up being sorted twice while the other 1024 half remains unsorted).

_No response_

[ARGSORT] ERR = 0.999998560 > 0.000000100   ARGSORT(type=f32,ne=[2048,1,1,1],order=0): FAIL
[ARGSORT] ERR = 0.999998601 > 0.000000100   ARGSORT(type=f32,ne=[2048,1,1,1],order=0): FAIL

Confirmed on desktop RDNA3 against master (`a02c7f58c`) — the exact repro passes on both my devices:

- Ryzen 7 7800X3D iGPU (RADV RAPHAEL_MENDOCINO, 1024): OK — also `ne=[4096,1,1,1]` OK

Root cause looks like the `pipeline_idx` clamp in `ggml_vk_argsort`:

```cpp
uint32_t pipeline_idx = std::min(ncols_pad_log2, num_argsort_pipelines - 1); // num_argsort_pipelines = 11
bool use_small = ncols_pad_log2 <= ctx->device->max_workgroup_size_log2 &&
                 ctx->device->pipeline_argsort_f32[pipeline_idx] != nullptr;
```

With `ne0 = 2048` (log2 = 11) on a device whose `max_workgroup_size_log2` is 11, `pipeline_idx` clamps to 10 (BLOCK_SIZE 1024), `pipeline[10]` exists, so `use_small` becomes true although that pipeline only covers 1024 columns — the cross-workgroup merge loop sits behind `if (!use_small)` and is skipped, and the dispatch runs 2 x 1024-wide workgroups over one row.

Broken window: `ne0` in (1024, 2048] on devices advertising 2048 invocations. Devices with 1024 limits (desktop RDNA) fall to the large path, hence PASS here.

Suggested fix: gate `use_small` on the unclamped index (require `ncols_pad_log2 == pipeline_idx`) so a clamped pipeline can never select the small path.

query:
server: speculative decoding keeps accepted tokens past the EOG, costing the whole previous answer on hybrid models

### Name and Version

version: 0.3.0-dev (build 252, commit 6b39dd5d5)
built with GNU 16.1.1 for Linux x86_64

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --alias qwen38 -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf \
  -ngl 999 -fa on -ub 2048 -b 2048 -c 204800 -np 1 -cram 32768 \
  --slot-save-path <dir> \
  --spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod --spec-draft-n-max 12 --spec-ngram-mod-n-min 24 \
  --chat-template-kwargs {"enable_thinking":false} \
  --jinja --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**Symptom.** With `draft-mtp` speculation on a hybrid model, every follow-up
request re-prefills the entire previous answer. Reuse stops exactly at the end
of the previous *prompt*. In live traffic the loss was consistently the answer
length **plus four tokens**: 16,791 lost where the answer was 16,787; 12,045
where it was 12,041; 1,503 where it was 1,499.

**What happens.** The accepted draft tokens are inserted into the slot in one
block, and only afterwards walked to find where the turn ends. The walk returns
early at the stop token and nothing removes the 1–2 accepted tokens behind it.
The slot is then no longer a prefix of the next prompt — `f_keep` reads 0.993
instead of 1.000.

On a model whose memory can be trimmed that is invisible. On a **hybrid /
recurrent** model it is not: the recurrent half cannot be rolled back to an
arbitrary position, so the server falls back to a context checkpoint. But
checkpoints are only created during prompt processing
(`checkpoint_offsets = {4 + n_ubatch, 4}`), never during generation — so the
newest usable one sits four tokens before the end of the *previous prompt*.
That is where the `+4` comes from.

**Steps to reproduce.** Any hybrid model with a draft head, `-np 1`:

1. Send a request, keep the answer.
2. Send it again with the answer appended and one more user turn.
3. Read the `selected slot by LCP similarity` line: `f_keep = 1.000` means the
   answer is kept, anything lower means it is about to be re-prefilled.

The tokens the slot keeps are **not visible in anything the server returns** —
`/completion` with `return_tokens` ends cleanly at `<|im_end|>`, and the usage
counts agree with it. Only `f_keep` shows them. That cost me several wrong
measurements before I noticed.

**Measured** (Qwen3.8-27B `qwen35`, hybrid attention+SSM, same binary each time,
one speculation type at a time):

| `--spec-type` | tokens kept past the turn | answer reused | decode, code |
|---|---|---|---|
| `draft-mtp,ngram-mod` | 2 (9 of 9 rounds) | 0 of 8 | 20.89 t/s |
| `draft-mtp` | 2 (2 of 4) | lost | 21.68 t/s |
| `ngram-mod` | 0 (4 of 4) | kept | 9.28 t/s |
| *(none)* | 0 (7 of 7) | kept | 9.06 t/s |

So it is `draft-mtp` specifically. `ngram-mod` does not produce the tail.

**Note on scope:** `qwen35` is on `llm_arch_supports_rs_rollback()`, `qwen4exp`
is not (see #28019) — so Qwen3.8-Flash-Next would hit the same thing once a
draft head exists for it, without even the rollback this model has.

**What I tried, and what it produced.** Removing the tokens *after* the walk
aborts the server. It needs a second `seq_rm` in the same step, and the
recurrent snapshot index is single-use — the draft verification has already
claimed it:

```
common.cpp:1628: failed to remove sequence 0 with p0=284, p1=-1
partial rollback REFUSED: rollback=3, n_rs_seq=12, pending=1 (rs_idx=6)
```

(The second line is from a local debug print I added; it does not exist
upstream. Note the numbers — the ring was 12 and the request was 3, so the
budget was never the constraint. The reservation was.)

Cutting `accepted` at the first EOG *before* `n_rollback` is computed works
instead, because then the one rollback the step already performs simply covers
those tokens too. Seven lines, between the `GGML_ASSERT(accepted.size() >= 1)`
and the `n_rollback` line in `update_slots`:

```c
for (size_t k = 0; k + 1 < accepted.size(); ++k) {
    if (llama_vocab_is_eog(vocab, accepted[k])) {
        accepted.resize(k + 1);
        break;
    }
}
```

The last element is the token sampled from the target model and is allowed to
be EOG — there is nothing behind it to drop.

On this machine that gives:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| tokens kept past the turn | 2 (9 of 9) | 0 (19 of 19) |
| previous answer reused | 0 of 8 | 12 of 13 |
| decode, code / prose | 20.89 / 8.52 t/s | 21.17 / 8.48 t/s |
| draft acceptance | 0.3347 (n=34) | 0.3334 (n=27) |

I am running that change on this machine now. To be precise about how much
that is worth: it has been in service for well under an hour, so the evidence
is the measurements above and not operating hours — 19 rounds with the tail
gone, 13 rounds of the reuse suite, one four-turn conversation, and no aborts
or rollback refusals in any of them. I will report back if anything shows up
over the coming days.

I am reporting this rather than opening a PR: I am a product engineer, not a
C++ developer, and I could not maintain the change. The measurements are
reproducible on my hardware and I am happy to run anything else that would
help — a different model, a different `--spec-draft-n-max`, longer sessions.

**AI usage disclosure:** the investigation and this report were done with AI
assistance. Every number above was measured on my machine and re-run; the
conclusions were checked against the source. I cannot vouch for a patch as my
own work, which is why this is an issue and not a pull request.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Both code paths are unchanged in master 9723942ad, so it is not a recent regression as far as I can tell.

### Relevant log output

slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.956 (> 0.100 thold), f_keep = 0.993
slot   operator(): id  0 | task 74 | old: ...  | <|endoftext|><|im_start|>      248044  248045
slot   operator(): id  0 | task 74 | new: ...  | <|im_start|>user               248045     846
slot   operator(): id  0 | task 74 | checking checkpoint with [46, 46] against 281...
slot   operator(): id  0 | task 74 | restored context checkpoint (pos_min = 46, pos_max = 46, n_tokens = 47, n_past = 47)
